entities.summary:
Leonardo Patrasso (1311-12-15) was a prominent Italian Franciscan and Cardinal who played a pivotal role in the Catholic Church during the medieval period. A key figure associated with the rise of the Papal States, Patrasso's influence extended to various aspects of Church governance and theological debates.

Patrasso's tenure as Cardinal saw him participate in several high-profile events, including the Conclave of 1313 and the Council of Vienne (1311-1312). These gatherings had significant implications for the Catholic Church, shaping its doctrine and organizational structure. Patrasso's contributions to these discussions further solidified his reputation as a respected voice within the Church.

Following his death, Patrasso's legacy continued to influence the development of Catholic theology and politics. His work on canonical law and liturgical reforms had lasting impacts on Church practices, shaping the rituals and governance structures that remained in place for centuries.

The sheer magnitude of Patrasso's impact cannot be overstated: he played a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of the Catholic faith, ensuring its continued relevance in an ever-changing world. As one of the most influential figures of his era, Patrasso left an indelible mark on the course of Church history.

Patrasso's commitment to upholding the principles of the Franciscan Order and his unwavering dedication to the Catholic faith have made him a revered figure in the annals of Church history. His remarkable story serves as a testament to the enduring power of faith, inspiring generations to come.
